Delhi-based ASF Group has so far delivered more than 5 million sq ft of workspaces across Northern India, PTI reported. In a statement on Wednesday, ASF group said it has leased about 0.4 million sq ft of office space at its project ‘ASF Insignia’, to Genpact. The transaction will see Genpact occupy a complete commercial tower. The company did not share the monthly rental for this leasing deal. It also did not disclose the tenure of the agreement. The project ‘ASF Insignia’, spread over 50 acres, is an IT office campus covering 4.5 million sq ft of premium office space. According to real estate consultant Vestian, the office space leasing rose 27 per cent to 23.9 million sq ft in June quarter of this year across seven major cities-Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad, Delhi-NCR, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.

The shift comes as institutional and private capital plays a larger role in real estate financing. Investors are increasingly tracking whether sales translate into timely collections, whether those funds are deployed efficiently towards construction and whether projects can meet financial commitments without repeated refinancing. Market observers said that, for investors, early repayment can offer a broader view of project execution than headline sales figures. It indicates whether a project is generating sufficient collections to fund construction while meeting financial obligations within its planned lifecycle. Several real estate developers have paid their debts early than their scheduled timeline across different micro-markets in Mumbai Metropolitan Region and Delhi NCR. “An early debt repayment is ultimately a result of these processes working together across sales, customer management, construction and finance,” said Amit Paranjape, director-business development, Paranjape Schemes (Construction) Limited. Paranjape Aspire, a residential project by Paranjape Schemes (Construction) Ltd, repaid its outstanding structured-credit facility to Arbour Investments on June 30, 2026, around six months ahead of schedule. The repayment was funded entirely through project receivables generated from home sales and construction progress. Arbour had sanctioned a Rs 35-crore facility, although only part of the facility was eventually drawn as project sales generated sufficient cash flows. Experts said that the ability to repay debt ahead of schedule demonstrates the ability to manage that capital efficiently. Market observers said that as real estate financing becomes more institutionalised, investors are likely to place greater emphasis on collections, construction progress, repayment records and refinancing requirements alongside bookings and sales value. They said that bookings, sales value and project size tell only part of the story. What matters is whether sales translate into timely collections, efficient deployment and stable project cash flows. Vishal Raheja, Founder & Managing Director, InvestoXpert Advisors said that early debt repayment is increasingly becoming an important indicator of a developer’s financial discipline and the quality of project cash flows. He said in real estate, bookings alone do not establish financial strength; the critical test is how efficiently sales convert into collections and whether those cash flows can fund construction, service debt and reduce leverage without repeated refinancing. “For investors, an early debt exit can signal stronger cash-flow conversion, better working-capital management and lower refinancing risk. As institutional capital gains a larger role in real estate, the ability to deleverage through internal project cash flows could increasingly become a key component of developer credibility and investor risk assessment,” he said. Representative image Housing prices in the Delhi-NCR primary market rose by a maximum of 12 per cent annually during the July-September period, driven by higher input costs and builders' increased focus on luxury projects, according to real estate consultant Anarock. Anarock data showed that average residential prices in Delhi-NCR increased to INR 9,980 per sq ft in the July-September quarter, from INR 8,900 per sq ft in the year-ago period. Across the top seven cities taken together, the average residential property price grew 7 per cent annually, to INR 9,714 per sq ft from INR 9,105 per sq ft. Among the top seven cities, Delhi-NCR recorded the highest annual jump, at 12 per cent. The top seven cities are Bengaluru, the Mumbai Metropolitan Region (MMR), Delhi-NCR, Pune, Chennai, Hyderabad and Kolkata. Anarock Vice Chairman Santhosh Kumar noted that housing prices have risen sharply since the pandemic across all major cities because of an increase in the cost of inputs, including land and construction raw materials. In Delhi-NCR, land rates in Noida, Greater Noida and Gurugram have surged, as reflected in auctions conducted by the development authorities, he said. Kumar added that developers are now focusing on launching premium, luxury and ultra-luxury homes only. On the demand and price trend, Manik Malik, CEO and President of BPTP Ltd, said housing demand remains steady. He said evolving infrastructure, connectivity and employment-led demand continue to support residential activity in NCR, particularly in the premium and luxury segments. Robin Mangla, President of M3M India, said sales in NCR saw a marginal moderation during the quarter, while the 12 per cent annual appreciation in residential prices reflects the continued strength of the market and the premium commanded by well-connected micro-markets. Ashish Sarin, CEO and Director of Alpha Corp Development Ltd, said the performance of the residential real estate market in the September quarter reflects the resilience of housing demand amid evolving global and economic conditions. He said strong end-user demand continues to support sales, with housing increasingly being viewed as a long-term need rather than purely an investment avenue. The Anarock figures place Delhi-NCR ahead of the other six major markets on price growth, at a time when development authorities in Noida, Greater Noida and Gurugram have continued to hold land auctions. rehydration.articleText: Thousands of residents of Chandigarh’s rehabilitation colonies may soon get legal ownership rights to their houses. The Chandigarh Administration is awaiting approval from the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) for a new policy covering properties sold through general power of attorney (GPA), wills or related agreements. The policy has been drafted after a fresh review of the Supreme Court’s November 2011 judgment in the Suraj Lamp case and has been sent to the MHA for approval. During a recently held grievance redressal programme at Ram Darbar, Punjab Governor and UT Administrator Gulab Chand Kataria had said that he had met Union Home Minister Amit Shah in Delhi and that residents would soon get “good news” on the issue. More than 34,000 houses have been constructed under various rehabilitation schemes in Chandigarh, and a large number of their present occupants had purchased the properties through GPA arrangements. Residents have been demanding legal ownership rights for years. Officials said a committee was constituted to examine the issue and recommend a framework for granting ownership rights. Based on its recommendations, the proposal was sent to the MHA. The committee also studied similar models adopted in other cities and examined legal aspects and court cases relating to such property transfers. Allotments of houses in the rehabilitation colonies were made over the years by the Estate Office and the Chandigarh Housing Board under various rehabilitation schemes. This is not the first attempt to resolve the issue. In 2023, another committee had been constituted to examine the matter. However, the administration did not accept its recommendations, stating that their implementation could create further complications for residents. A fresh committee was subsequently formed to prepare a more practical and legally viable proposal. The administration also conducted a survey of houses in rehabilitation colonies across the city. According to the survey, more than 80 per cent of the occupants are not the original allottees. They are residing in houses purchased through GPA. In several cases, officials found that houses had changed hands multiple times through informal agreements. The houses were allotted under rehabilitation schemes beginning in 1979, mostly on a 99-year lease basis. However, after the Supreme Court order on property transfers through GPA transactions in 2011, residents who had purchased houses through such arrangements were left facing legal uncertainty. Residents of various colonies, including Dadumajra, Indira Colony, Mauli Jagran, Dhanas, Bapu Dham, Manimajra and Sectors 52 and 56, have been seeking ownership rights for years. The officials said granting ownership rights would provide legal security to thousands of families and significantly enhance the value of the properties. According to official data, 34,965 houses have been constructed in Chandigarh under rehabilitation schemes. These houses were allotted to economically weaker sections either on a leasehold basis or against monthly licence fees. Under the proposed policy, GPA holders seeking registration of their properties will have to pay stamp duty based on the prevailing collector rate of the area. In addition, buyers will have to pay an “unearned increase” to the administration. The administration is expected to formulate a detailed mechanism for calculating the charges once the proposal receives final approval from the MHA.
